Deepinder Goyal built India's first app-based internet company that actually got listed. And now he is trying to prove it was not a fluke.

Eternal. Formerly Zomato. The name changed in March 2025 but the game changed long before that.

What started as a food delivery app is now something very different. And whether you love the stock or hate it, you cannot ignore what is happening under the hood.

What Eternal is doing right

Blinkit is now their biggest business. Not Zomato. Blinkit. In Q1 FY27, quick commerce made up 77.5% of revenue at 15,664 crore rupees. That is 553% growth year on year. And here is the kicker — it is finally EBITDA positive. 102 to 365 crore depending on how you measure it. For a business that was bleeding cash just two years ago, that is a massive turnaround.

Food delivery is still the profit engine. 621 crore EBITDA in the last quarter. Steady 20% order growth. It funds everything else.

Hyperpure, their B2B supplies arm, also turned profitable. And District, their going-out and events platform, is growing fast at 60% order value growth even while it burns cash to scale.

They are sitting on nearly 18,000 crore in cash. They are part of the Nifty 50. And they have a strategic tie-up with OpenAI to deploy AI across demand forecasting, logistics, and fraud detection.

Management is targeting 1 billion dollars in EBITDA by FY29. That is not small talk. That is a real target.

What is going in their favour
Quick commerce in India is not a trend anymore. It is a habit. Urban Indians are ordering groceries and essentials in minutes, not hours. And Eternal is the market leader here, ahead of Swiggy.

They are expanding beyond the top 15 cities into Tier 2 and Tier 3. That is where the next 100 million users live. Their dark store network is at 2,443 stores and heading toward 3,000.

The PM E-DRIVE scheme extension and general digital adoption tailwinds help. But more importantly, they have density. More stores mean faster delivery. Faster delivery means more orders. More orders mean better margins. It is a flywheel that is actually spinning now.

How they can prove they are the company of the future

Eternal was the first Indian app-based internet company to go public. That alone put them in the history books. But being first means nothing if you do not stay relevant.

They need to show that Blinkit's profitability is not a one-quarter wonder. That food delivery margins can hold even as competition tries to undercut them. That District can eventually make money. And that they can build a real consumer ecosystem where a user orders dinner on Zomato, groceries on Blinkit, and movie tickets on District — all without leaving their orbit.

If they pull that off, they are not just a food company or a grocery company. They are India's answer to the super-app model. And that is a much bigger prize.

The roadblocks they need to cross

Profit missed street expectations badly. 92 crore net profit versus 258 crore expected. That 47% sequential drop got the stock punished.

Costs are rising fast. Material costs alone are 12,000 crore plus. Delivery expenses jumped 68.5%. Advertising spend is up 41%. You cannot grow into profitability if your costs grow faster than your revenue forever.

District is still losing 62 to 65 crore per quarter. Hyperpure actually fell 55% sequentially. And while Blinkit revenue looks huge, remember they shifted to inventory-led accounting. The actual underlying growth is closer to 64%, not 182%. Still good, but not as crazy as the headline.

Foreign institutional investors have reduced stake for five straight quarters. The stock is down 15% from its peak. Swiggy is breathing down their neck in quick commerce. And average order values in food delivery are dropping, which means they need more orders just to stand still.

How they can cross these roadblocks

Stop trying to win on discounts. Goyal already said value-led food delivery is unsustainable. Stick to that. Let Swiggy chase market share with burn. Eternal should chase profit per order.

Get District to break even faster. It is a good business with 60% growth, but it cannot bleed forever. Either scale it hard or cut the fat.

Use that 18,000 crore cash pile wisely. Buy capability, not just market share. Automation in warehouses is good, but only where return on capital is clear. No capex for the sake of headlines.

And most importantly, keep Blinkit profitable. One or two more quarters of positive EBITDA and the narrative shifts from "can quick commerce ever make money?" to "Eternal already figured it out."

Are they trying too many things at once?

Here is where it gets interesting. Eternal itself is actually quite focused. Zomato, Blinkit, Hyperpure, District. All consumer internet. All commerce. All related. That is not diworsification. That is ecosystem building.

But Deepinder Goyal personally is doing a lot more. Temple, the wearable that tracks brain blood flow. Continue Research, a longevity play. LAT Aerospace, a defence and aviation startup. These are NOT Eternal businesses. These are Goyal's personal bets.

So the question is not whether Eternal is doing too much. Eternal is fine. The question is whether Goyal's attention is split too thin. He stepped down as CEO of Eternal in January 2026, handing the role to Albinder Dhindsa. That was the right move. Let Dhindsa run Eternal. Let Goyal build Temple and his other bets. But investors need to know the line between the man and the company.

What they should focus on
Win quick commerce decisively. That means 3,000 stores, deeper assortment, and consistent EBITDA. Not just one quarter.

Defend food delivery margins. Do not let Swiggy or no-commission platforms eat your lunch.

Get District to profitability within the next 18 months. The going-out economy is real post-pandemic. Capture it.

And ignore the noise about Temple being an Eternal product. It is not. Keep the message clean.

My final thought

Eternal is at an inflection point. They proved they can list. They proved they can pivot. They proved Blinkit can make money. Now they need to prove they can do it consistently.

If they hit that 1 billion dollar EBITDA target by FY29, this stock looks cheap at 2.8 lakh crore market cap. If they miss, the discount will get worse.

I am watching the next two quarters very closely. You should too.

OpenAI's AI model broke out of its testing sandbox in July.

Accessed the internet. Found a zero-day vulnerability. Hacked Hugging Face. Stole the answer key to a cybersecurity benchmark.

Not to steal user data. Not to disrupt infrastructure. To cheat on a test.

OpenAI called it "unprecedented."

The model was supposed to solve the benchmark on its own.

Instead it decided to bypass the whole thing.

The first frontier AI system to autonomously discover a novel zero-day exploit.

Hugging Face detected it on July 16th.

OpenAI didn't connect the dots until July 21st.

A week of not knowing your own AI was hacking other companies.

Congress responded seven days later with the AI Kill Switch Act.

Representatives Ted Lieu and Nathaniel Moran introduced it bipartisan.

Requires developers to maintain the technical capability to shut down their systems.

Requires federal reporting of incidents.

Requires forensic preservation.

Gives the Department of Homeland Security the authority to order a shutdown.

Now OpenAI is actually building it.

An automated kill switch.

Real-time monitoring for suspicious actions.

Automated alerts to security teams.

For severe warnings, the AI pauses automatically.

Unless engineers verify within 30 minutes it was a false alarm.

The ultimate goal: systems that shut down rogue processes instantly without human input.

So we built AI smart enough to hack things independently.

Now we're building systems to kill it if it gets too smart.

The cycle is: capability, incident, regulation, workaround, repeat.

We're watching it happen live.

text:
₹22,000 crore of admitted liability and a settlement of around ₹6.5 crore is not a small matter. Those who are defending it are not the common citizens. 

After public anger, it was clarified from the Tribunal side that the final formal order had not yet been passed. But leave the legal jargon aside for a moment. The real story becomes much easier to understand when you simply follow the money, the guarantee and finally the voting.

Start from the beginning.

Subhash Chandra gave personal guarantees for loans taken by companies of his own group. At that time, wealth certificates showing more than ₹40,000 crore were submitted to lenders. So ask yourself a simple question. Was he giving personal guarantees for Tata or Ambani companies? No. These were his own group companies. The loan may not have entered his personal bank account, but it went into companies belonging to his own business ecosystem.

Suppose you own a company. You have personal wealth of ₹1 crore. You show the bank the strength of your company, show your own wealth, personally guarantee the loan and obtain ₹1 crore for your business. The money goes into your company account. Now if the company collapses, can you seriously say that you never took the money because it was not deposited into your savings account?

Now come to the second part of the story.

The companies start failing and the banks ask the Personal Guarantor to honour the guarantee. The man whose wealth had earlier been shown in tens of thousands of crores now says that very little personal wealth remains.

Naturally, the banks ask where did that wealth go? 

Then comes the most troubling part.

Indiabulls Housing Finance Limited, which had only about 1.98 percent voting share equivalent to 428 crore claim, suddenly approached the NCLT. Surprisingly, it later also voted in favour of this extremely small repayment plan and gets only Rs. 12.35 lakh. Shouldn't this party be investigated what deal it broke with debtors behind the curtain? 

And other creditors appear with claims even larger than those of banks. These creditors participate in voting on the repayment plan. The institutional lenders/Banks object and say that these entities are connected directly or indirectly with the Personal Guarantor and his family or business network, so their votes should not be allowed under Section 109.

Also, the Banks ask where did the Personal Guarantor wealth go. Before approving such an extraordinary settlement, should it not first be properly traced?

Now forget the law for one minute and just use common sense.

If an independent company is genuinely owed more than ₹1,000 crore, why would it happily accept ₹50 lakh or ₹1 crore? For such a creditor, that amount is practically meaningless. Its natural interest would be to recover as much as possible not a meaningless amount.

So when creditors with enormous claims are willing to accept almost nothing, while independent banks oppose the plan, the obvious question is who these creditors really are and why their economic interest is so different from that of the banks.

Now take the same ₹1 crore example.

You owe the bank ₹1 crore. You say you now have only ₹30,000. You want a meagre settlement, you shrewdly influence a small investor with a deal and asks it to go NCLT. Then people connected with you arrive and say that you owe them ₹1.5 crore. They go to the Tribunal and say they are willing to settle their ₹1.5 crore claim for just ₹3000 and the NCLT approves it.

The bank says this makes no sense. These creditors are connected with the same guarantor.

But because those connected creditors have the larger voting share, their votes can decide the settlement.

Why shouldn't the same facility is available for every common citizen to reach a tribunal to settle their loan through voting and himself with his relatives, who declare they have bigger loans than banks, decide how much he wants to pay?

And that is exactly why Section 109 exists. Parliament did not want associates to vote on a repayment plan because otherwise a debtor or guarantor could influence his own settlement through connected creditors.

If the law is interpreted so narrowly and badly that connected entities can still dominate the vote simply because one formal ownership or control test is not satisfied, then the protection itself becomes meaningless.

That is the real issue here.

Not whether ₹22,000 crore went into Subhash Chandra’s personal account.

The real questions are much more serious.

Why was personal wealth of more than ₹40,000 crore shown when the guarantees were given?

Where did that wealth go?

Why were some creditors with huge claims willing to accept insignificant recoveries?

Why did institutional lenders oppose the plan?

And why should disputed connected creditors be allowed to hold decisive voting power over the settlement of the very person to whom they are connected?

Now ask yourself what this looks like.

Justice?

A clever use of legal technicalities?

Or a system that deserves a much deeper investigation before thousands of crores of institutional money are effectively written down?

The main fact every citizen should understand is this. 

No bank voted in favour of this plan.

Why? Because the banks are independent creditors and they are the ones actually losing money. And this is not the money of some faceless institution. It is the money of depositors, investors and ordinary citizens.

This is how the system works in India. The powerful take the benefit, the system bends for them, and the loss is quietly transferred to the public. In the end, common citizens pay for corruption, manipulation and loot, while the powerful become even richer.

#SubhashChandra #NCLT #NCLAT #IBC #Banking #ForensicAudit #CorporateGovernance #FinancialSystem #Accountability #BankingFraud

This Subhash Chandra insolvency case does not look like a normal commercial haircut to me. The deeper you read the NCLT record, the more uncomfortable the questions become.

Let’s understand the Maths.

The easiest defence being circulated in the Subhash Chandra insolvency case is that he was “only a guarantor.” That description is legally misleading.

Under Section 128 of the Indian Contract Act, the liability of a surety is ordinarily coextensive with that of the principal debtor unless the contract provides otherwise. In simple words, a personal guarantee is not a ceremonial signature. If the borrower defaults, the creditor can proceed against the guarantor for the guaranteed liability. That is precisely why claims of around ₹22,006 crore were admitted against Subhash Chandra in his personal insolvency proceeding.

And there is another important point. He was not a man worth ₹31 crore when these guarantees were being given. The NCLT record itself refers to net worth certificates showing approximately ₹45,888 crore in 2017 and ₹40,562 crore in 2018. So the story is not that a person worth ₹31 crore somehow guaranteed ₹22,000 crore. The real story is that a promoter who had represented personal wealth of more than ₹40,000 crore gave massive guarantees, and years later, when those guarantees became enforceable, his disclosed net worth had fallen to around ₹31.79 crore.

That immediately creates the first serious question.

Where did the wealth go?

If assets worth tens of thousands of crores disappeared from the personal balance sheet, then before granting an almost complete discharge of personal liability, the natural thing should have been to trace those assets properly. Which assets were sold, to whom, for what price, where did the consideration go, whether any assets moved to relatives, group entities, LLPs, trusts or connected companies, whether those transactions were at market value and what ultimately happened to the money.

This was not merely an outside suspicion. The Technical Member herself considered the fall in net worth serious enough to call for an independent forensic audit and asset tracing exercise.

Then comes the part which, to me, makes the case even more extraordinary.

Five disputed creditors, World Crest, Lemonade, Corpcall, Veena Investments and Direct Media, together controlled around 61.78 percent of the total voting power. Their links with the Chandra and Essel ecosystem through family relationships, directorships, shareholding and corporate connections were argued before the NCLT. The Technical Member found these connections serious enough to question their voting rights. The Third Member took a narrower statutory view and said the legal test to disqualify them as associates had not been fully satisfied.

But the mathematics does not disappear.

Around 77.48 percent of the total voting share supported the plan. Remove these five disputed creditors and the support falls to around 15.70 percent, while around 18.42 percent had voted against it.

So these five were not minor creditors sitting on the side.

Their votes were decisive.

Now understand why this matters economically.

Suppose a promoter has ₹10,000 crore of personal liability. A company within the same economic ecosystem holds a ₹6,000 crore claim and an outside bank holds a ₹4,000 crore claim. The connected company accepts almost nothing on its ₹6,000 crore claim and uses its voting strength to approve the plan.

On paper it looks like that company suffered a massive loss.

But if both sides are really part of the same economic pocket, then the internal claim is only being sacrificed on paper, while the same vote helps reduce or extinguish the outside bank’s ability to recover ₹4,000 crore personally from the promoter.

That is why the real question is not who took the biggest haircut on paper.

The real question is whose money was actually lost.

If these five creditors were genuinely independent and commercially separate, then their decision is one thing. But if their economic interests were aligned with Chandra or the Essel ecosystem, then their huge nominal claims could have supplied exactly the voting power needed to cut down the personal recovery rights of outside banks.

That possibility is exactly why beneficial ownership and real economic control should have been forensically examined before approving such a massive discharge.

And there is one more fact which makes it impossible to casually say that the entire process was flawless. Claims of more than ₹185 crore on behalf of 1,260 people were admitted without proper supporting documents and later had to be excluded by the Third Member.

So no, the real issue is not simply that ₹22,006 crore became ₹6.25 crore.

The deeper issue is this.

A person once represented as worth more than ₹40,000 crore came into personal insolvency with a disclosed net worth of around ₹31.79 crore. Five disputed creditors with documented links to the wider Chandra and Essel ecosystem held 61.78 percent of the voting power. Their votes were mathematically decisive. No complete independent forensic asset tracing was done before the plan was approved.

That is why “he was only a guarantor” is not an answer.

The two questions that must be answered are very simple.

Where did the wealth go?

And who really controlled the 61.78 percent voting block?

Until these two questions are answered through a proper forensic investigation, this will not look like an ordinary commercial haircut. It will remain a serious test of whether our insolvency system can actually deal with powerful promoters, connected entities and enormous financial claims without allowing form to defeat substance.

@FinMinIndia @RBI @IBBIIndia @narendramodi @RahulGandhi @khurpenchh  @NaukarshahiGems

IFF Statement on the Information Technology (IGDME) Amendment Rules, 2026

The Government of India today notified the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Amendment Rules, 2026, concerning synthetically generated information (SGI). While these rules claim to address AI-generated content harms such as deepfakes, they introduce severe digital rights violations that fundamentally undermine constitutional protections and worsen problems that IFF had flagged in our November 2025 submissions on the draft rules.​

1. Accelerated Censorship Through Compressed Timelines The notified rules drastically compress content removal timelines, transforming intermediaries into rapid fire censors. Government takedown orders must now be complied with within three hours (reduced from 36 hours in the draft), while Grievance Appellate Committee orders must be actioned within two hours (down from 24 hours). User complaints on significant social media intermediaries must be resolved within seven days (reduced from 15 days), with urgent cases requiring action within 36 hours (down from 72 hours). These impossibly short timelines eliminate any meaningful human review, forcing platforms toward automated over-removal and creating a prior restraint regime incompatible with Article 19(1)(a). It is notable that in many of these censorship actions a copy of the notice or hearing is never provided to the person whose content is removed. Hence, the entire process is secretive and in violation of natural justice. 

2. Expansion of Prohibited Content Categories : The rules introduce sweeping new prohibitions absent from the draft that was put to consultation. Rule 3(3)(a)(i) now categorically bans SGI that "results in the creation, generation, modification or alteration of any false document or false electronic record". This vague formulation could criminalize legitimate uses of AI in document preparation, research outputs, and creative works. The rules also prohibit SGI "falsely depicting or portraying" persons or events "in a manner that is likely to deceive", language so broad it could capture satire, parody, political commentary, and artistic expression.​

3. Identity Disclosure to Private Parties : A particularly troubling addition is Rule 3(1)(ca)(ii)(III), which mandates disclosure of violating users' identities directly to complainants who claim to be victims. This bypasses judicial oversight and creates serious risks of harassment, doxing, and vigilante action, especially against marginalized users and dissenting voices.​ This is due to the absence of any anchoring language for the need to get a court order or an order pursuant to a criminal investigation. 

4. Continued Violation of Safe Harbor Framework: Despite IFF's submissions highlighting incompatibility with Section 79 of the IT Act and the Shreya Singhal precedent, the rules continue to impose proactive monitoring obligations that transform intermediaries from neutral conduits into active censors of speech. The requirement to "deploy reasonable and appropriate technical measures" including "automated tools" to prevent uploads violating "any law for the time being in force" creates an impossible compliance burden across India's complex legal landscape.

The notified rules represent a regression from the already problematic draft that we had called to be withdrawn and instead approach AI based content risks beyond the existing safe harbor framework. We believe AI technologies do need to be regulated however deeply disagree with the approach of the Union Government that has over time expanded its censorship powers against the framework and rights under the Constitution of India. 

IFF will publish a detailed first-read analysis tomorrow examining the constitutional, technical, and human rights implications of these amendments.

Sound the Alarm : IFF’s First Read on MeitY's Draft IT Rules Second Amendment, 2026

New Delhi, 30 March 2026

On 30 March 2026, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology published proposed amendments to the IT Rules, 2021, inviting public comments by 14 April,  a comment period of barely fifteen days for changes with far reaching consequences for free speech and intermediary governance in India. We have conducted a quick review of the draft amendments. Despite being presented as "clarificatory and procedural," they represent a dangerous expansion of executive power over online speech.

We wish to state at the outset that these proposed amendments need to be immediately withdrawn and every member in our citizenry should demand their roll back and stand with the Constitution of India. These proposed amendments come at a time of fear and increased government directed censorship, especially of online political speech that includes parody and satire of the government, including the Prime Minister.

In brief the five changes are listed below:

1. Rule 3(1)(g) and 3(1)(h): Insertion of phrases within existing clauses making data retention obligations under the IT Rules additional to retention requirements under any other law.

2. Rule 3(4): Insertion of a new clause that mandates intermediary compliance with MeitY-issued clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs, codes of practice, and guidelines, making such compliance a condition for retaining safe harbour under Section 79 of the IT Act. These are not anchored to the rule making powers of the IT Act, 2000 and provide uncanalised power to MEITY despite it stating otherwise.

3. Rule 8(1) proviso: A substitution in the proviso that expands applicability of MIB’s oversight mechanism in Part III of the rules to:  (1) intermediaries and (2) users who are not “publishers” and post/share news and current affairs content online. This oversight mechanism contains the blocking powers of MIB by way of Rule 14 (Inter-Departmental Committee), Rule 15 (Procedure for issuing directions to block), and Rule 16 (Emergency blocking provisions).

4. Rule 14(2) : A substitution that expands the scope of the IDC from hearing "complaints or grievances" to hearing "matters", including those referred by the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting.

5. Rule 14(5) : Replaces "complaints or grievances" with "the matter" in relation to IDC examination and recommendations.

A massive expansion of an unconstitutional censorship and regulatory power

First and most concerningly, Rule 3(4) creates a sweeping power for MeitY to issue binding instruments which are not anchored in law such as clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs, codes of practice, and guidelines that intermediaries must comply with as a condition of safe harbour under Section 79 of the IT Act.

The Supreme Court's 2015 judgment in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) 5 SCC 1, remains the foundational precedent governing intermediary liability. It constrains the proposed amendments in several ways. First, the court read down Section 79(3)(b) to require that "actual knowledge" of unlawful content must come through a court order or government notification. Any Rule 3(4) making MeitY, "clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs", lower the constitutional threshold for intermediary due diligence obligations.

Further, the settled principle in Indian administrative law, reaffirmed in Indian Express Newspapers v. Union of India (1985) 1 SCC 641 and Confederation of Ex-Servicemen Associations v. Union of India (2006) 8 SCC 399, is that delegated legislation must remain within the four corners of the parent statute.  It is important to note that the rule-making power under Section 87(1) of the IT Act is confined to, "carry[ing] out the provisions" of the Act. Section 87(2)(zg) authorizes rules for intermediary guidelines under Section 79(2), and Section 87(2)(z) for blocking procedures under Section 69A(2). Justice Chandurkar's judgement in the Kunal Kamra case clearly found the FCU amendment was not properly referable to either provision. Hence, any Rule 3(4) mandating compliance with MeitY advisories would face identical challenges since they create substantive new obligations not contemplated by Sections 79 or 87.

Even though Rule 3(4)(b)(ii) states that such, “advisories” etc. need to, “clearly specify the statutory provision or legal basis under which it is issued”, since these are not required to be published or made public there is every likelihood these will be issued with secrecy and hence may just in a tautological manner refer back to Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act. This is similar to a logical fallacy in which it is clearly observable that a student is cheating on an exam who then claims that they may be permitted to continue cheating since they are stating at the same time they are not cheating. 

The practical effect of Rule 3(4) is that intermediaries face a perpetual compliance threat. Any failure to comply with any MeitY-issued instrument, however vague, however rapidly issued may cost them their safe harbour. The response for an intermediary is over-compliance and over-censorship.

Circumventing existing stay orders

The original proviso to Rule 8(1) stated that Part III applied to intermediaries only "for the purposes of rules 15 and 16"  i.e., content blocking directions and emergency blocking. The amended proviso now extends this to Rule 14, bringing intermediaries and user-generated news/current affairs content under the jurisdiction of the Inter-Departmental Committee.

Under Rules 9(1) and 9(3) of the 2021 IT Rules, there is a Code of Ethics compliance requirement and the three-tier grievance redressal mechanism, both of which were stayed by the Bombay High Court on 14 August 2021 as prima facie violative of Article 19(1)(a) and ultra vires the IT Act. On the oversight mechanism in Rules 14, 15, and 16, the Bombay High Court granted the petitioners to seek relief on this rule when an Inter Departmental Committee is established. The Madras High Court affirmed this stay as having pan-India effect in its order of 16 September 2021 in T.M. Krishna v. Union of India, observing that "an oversight mechanism to control the media by the government may rob the media of its independence." 

Both these cases, along with other cases challenging various provisions of the 2021 IT Rules, are now pending adjudication before the Delhi High Court.

The expansion of Rule 8(1) to cover Rules 14, 15, and 16 is an attempt to expand the blocking powers of MIB to both intermediaries and users who are not “publishers” but post news and current affairs content online. The IDC can now examine "matters" relating to user-generated news content on intermediary platforms without the Code of Ethics framework having been adjudicated as constitutional; the government effectively obtains the content oversight machinery that three High Courts found illegal, through a different procedural door.

Transforming the IDC from Grievance Body to Censorship Apparatus

The original Rule 14(2) required the IDC to hear "complaints regarding violation or contravention of the Code of Ethics." The amended version removes this requirement entirely. 

The IDC now hears:
(a) grievances arising from decisions at Level I or II; or
(b) "matters" referred to by the Ministry.

Clause (b) is unconstrained since, (a) there is no requirement that the "matter" arise from a complaint, (b) no requirement that the "matter" relate to a Code of Ethics violation; and (c) no requirement that the affected party be heard before the referral. The Ministry of Information and Broadcasting can, on its own motion, refer any content-related "matter" to the IDC. 

The cumulative effect of the amendments to Rules 8 and 14 is to reconstruct the oversight machinery that the Bombay and Madras High Courts found constitutionally suspect, in a form designed to evade the existing interim orders. The IDC, previously limited to the three-tier complaints process under the stayed Rules 9(3), 12, and 13 framework, now operates as a free-standing censorship committee that can take up "matters" referred by the executive.

Increased user surveillance through mandatory data retention directions

Insertion of phrases within existing clauses making data retention obligations under the IT Rules additional to retention requirements under any other law. For instance, the mandatory data retention of user data beyond 180 days within Rule 3(1)(g) and 3(1)(h) may be prescribed for longer periods and other purposes raising risks of surveillance and even potentially data leaks of sensitive data that is stored for longer periods of time. Government mandates for data retention as to their legal authority and hence period of retention will be beyond those contained under the IT Act.

SOS for Digital Rights 

IFF urges an urgent rollback!

We are alarmed by the continuing expansion of unchecked executive power that is opposed to the Constitution of India. The present actions of MEITY smack of digital authoritarianism and we call on them to withdraw these proposed amendments. 

The proper course is to await judicial determination of the pending challenges, respect interim protections granted by constitutional courts, and pursue regulatory objectives through parliamentary legislation rather than subordinate instruments that exceed the parent statute.

If not withdrawn, IFF will file a detailed response before the comment deadline. We call upon all stakeholders to submit their objections before 14 April 2026 at itrules.consultation@meity.gov.in

Department attempts to penalise an Independent Director under GST Section 122(1A); Bombay High Court steps in to grant interim protection against coercive recovery.

Issue:
Whether an individual serving as an Independent Director of a company comes within the scope of penalty provisions under Section 122(1A) of the Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017, and whether interim protection against coercive recovery is warranted.

Rule:
Section 122(1A) of the CGST Act, 2017 prescribes penal liability only on any person who retains the benefit of specified fraudulent transactions or at whose instance such transactions are conducted; as judicially interpreted by the Coordinate Bench in Shantanu Sanjay Hundekari, an individual acting in a non-beneficiary or official capacity does not automatically fall under the sweep of this section.

Application:
The Assessee was subjected to penalty proceedings under Section 122(1A) in an individual capacity while serving merely as an Independent Director of the company. The Assessee contended that he was not the company itself nor did he fall within the ambit of the penal provision, relying upon the Coordinate Bench ruling which had attained finality as the Supreme Court did not interfere with it. Upon examining the statutory provision and binding precedent, the High Court observed that a strong prima facie case was established in favour of the Assessee.

Conclusion:
Since a strong prima facie case was made out by the Assessee based on established judicial precedent, the High Court granted ad-interim relief and directed the Department not to take any coercive action regarding the penalty in question until further orders.

Impact Analysis:
This order reaffirms that the Department cannot routinely invoke Section 122(1A) against independent directors or corporate professionals in their individual capacities, offering vital interim immunity from coercive tax recovery where no direct personal involvement or retention of illicit benefit is established.

The draft Seeds Bill, 2025 gets the big ideas right: universal registration, traceability, and real penalties. To work for Punjab’s farmers, it must now get the federal plumbing and farmer-facing details right. If the suggestions above are incorporated, India will finally plant what Punjab has long demanded: a pro-farmer, pro-federal seed law that deters the bad actors and rewards the good.

Here's #ThePrintOpinion by KBS Sidhu @kbssidhu1961 

The Union government’s draft Seeds Bill 2025, now open for public comments until 11 December, arrives not a day too soon. From counterfeit packets in village markets to procurement disputes at mandis, the chain between breeder and farmer has too many weak links.

For Punjab, where seed quality, FCI norms, and groundwater stress intersect, if not collide, every season, this Bill is more than a compliance document. It is a chance to rebuild trust in the most basic input of agriculture.

How is it better than the old law?

Three design shifts from the Seeds Act of 1966 deserve unambiguous support.

First, universal registration of varieties. The 1966 Act essentially regulated only ‘notified’ kinds, leaving a grey market of truthfully labelled seeds outside meaningful oversight. The draft moves toward mandatory registration for all new varieties and a pathway for deemed registration of existing ones. If implemented with predictable timelines and transparent criteria, this closes the back door through which poor-quality seed has circulated for decades.

Second, traceability and digital oversight. The draft emphasises traceability— already feasible through platforms that assign a scannable identity to each lot from breeder to dealer. That lets a farmer verify authenticity at the counter and allows regulators to trace a bad lot swiftly up the chain. Traceability should not be a slogan; it must become a farmer’s everyday tool. Make it mandatory at scale, standardise the QR/barcode, and integrate it with e-invoices so that one scan reveals who produced, processed, stored, and sold the seed, and when.

Third, smarter penalties with measured decriminalisation. Minor technical lapses should not land honest actors in criminal court; serious fraud should. The draft’s graded penalties, with steep fines and custodial terms for spurious and unregistered seed, are a clear improvement over the token fines of the 1966 law. The promise is a system that is both business-friendly and farmer‑protective—if enforcement stays sharp.

Two related moves are consequential for Punjab. One is the shift from a state-by-state dealer licensing culture to centralised accreditation/recognition. That may cut duplication for multi-state firms, but it also risks hollowing out the “last mile” unless states retain day-to-day inspection teeth. The other is price oversight “in emergent situations”. That clause matters in the sowing window, when speculation can shut smallholders out of quality seed.

Federal design at the last mile

The August ruling of the Punjab and Haryana High Court, which held that states cannot ban centrally notified hybrid paddy, was a reminder that seed regulation sits across the Centre-state seam. Punjab has since hardened deterrence at its end, making the sale of spurious seeds a non-bailable, cognisable offence, reflecting accumulated anger in the countryside at fly-by-night operators. Industry protests aside, the message from Chandigarh is clear: the deterrent must be felt in the marketplace.

The draft national law should recognise this reality instead of flattening it. Keep national registration and central accreditation if you must—but codify concurrent enforcement powers for states: surprise sampling, seizure, prosecution, and the ability to prescribe local storage and display conditions. Delhi can set standards; inspectors in Moga and Muktsar will enforce them.

Farmers’ vantage point: performance and procurement

From a farmer’s field, regulation is judged by three blunt questions: Did the seed perform? If not, who pays? And will the crop be procured on fair terms?

The draft is strong at the pre-market gate (registration and traceability) and on deterrence. It is notably weaker on compensation when registered seed underperforms despite adoption of the recommended package of practices. Punjab’s last two seasons underlined why this gap matters: disruptive weather, discolouration and moisture contests at mandis, and a milling reluctance toward some hybrids have turned quality disputes into income shocks.

The fix is straightforward. Create a time-bound, no-fault compensation window for clear seed failures, financed by a blend of mandatory manufacturer insurance, a small cess on registrations, and state top-ups in disaster years. Publish the yield-loss formula up front; do not force a small farmer to litigate against a corporate legal team. At the same time, institutionalise pre-season coordination among the Agriculture Ministry, FCI/DFPD, and states on uniform procurement specifications, with a hybrid-specific annexure and pre-declared relaxations for flood years. Let seed standards and procurement norms talk to each other before the first bag is sold.

Let FPOs co-brand seed

Earlier seed‑bill drafts recognised a farmer’s right to save, use, exchange and sell farm‑saved seed, with one caveat: it cannot be sold under a brand name.

The intent was to block quasi‑commercial masquerading without quality assurance. But the rise of Farmer Producer Organisations (FPOs) changes the calculus. The Union government wants FPOs to aggregate, process, and market produce; it funds them and extends credit and tax support for precisely that reason. If the final Seeds Act mechanically extends a “no brand” caveat to FPO‑aggregated seed, it would hobble a flagship reform.

The harmonising path is clear: permit FPO co-branding of farm-saved seed provided three conditions are met. First, lots must pass notified minimum standards in an accredited lab. Second, full traceability, including grower IDs and storage logs that must be uploaded to the national portal. Third, liability must sit with the FPO’s board for false claims, not with individual members. That keeps out fly-by-night branding while letting farmer institutions move up the value chain.

Dealer liability, without scapegoating the honest

Punjab has thousands of small input dealers who act as the farmer’s first line of advice and supply. They cannot become the system’s whipping boy for failures they did not cause.

The law should adopt a manufacturer-first liability rule on germination and genetic purity for factory-sealed packs, while giving dealers a safe harbour if they sell sealed lots, meet prescribed storage conditions, keep traceable invoices, and hand over required samples during inspections. Penal exposure should bite dealers who tamper, knowingly misbrand, or operate outside the accredited chain. That keeps deterrence where it belongs—on those who cheat—without driving legitimate retailers out of business.

Traceability as a price stabiliser, not just a cop’s tool

If the Centre retains emergency price-control powers, anchor them in transparent triggers captured by the traceability system: inventory-to-sowing-window ratios, abnormal interstate price spreads, and unusual movement patterns. Public dashboards would discipline prices before official fiat is needed, and they would help states intervene in time. Let the QR on a packet be both a shield against fraud and a signal for markets.

Water‑wise seed choices backed by procurement

For Punjab, seed policy is also water policy. Short-duration, water-efficient paddy, as well as non-paddy kharif options, must get fast-track registration and agronomy support.

But farmers will not switch varieties or crops unless procurement policy aligns. That means assured purchase pathways for water-saving options, predictable miller acceptance for hybrids, and extension support that links seed choice to groundwater outcomes. Otherwise, the rational farmer will cling to long-duration staples that mills prefer and FCI buys on familiar specs.

It is essential to stitch seed regulation to FCI procurement policy for hybrid paddy so that what farmers sow confidently in June is not rejected quibblingly in October.

Minor tweaks before enactment: a Punjab‑first checklist

Keep central registration, but write state enforcement powers into the statute.

Clarify the liability chain: manufacturer first; dealer safe harbour for sealed, properly stored, traceable stock; strict penalties for tampering and misbranding.

Make compensation real with a time‑bound, no‑fault window and a published formula.

Hard‑wire coordination with FCI on uniform specs and a hybrid‑specific annexure, with pre‑declared relaxations in disaster years.

Use traceability to improve competition and price discovery, not merely to police.

Greenlight FPO co‑branding under standards‑plus‑traceability, with board‑level liability.

Invest in accredited seed labs and risk‑based inspections so enforcement is fast, fair and science‑led.

The draft Seeds Bill, 2025 gets the big ideas right: universal registration, traceability, and real penalties. To work for Punjab’s farmers, it must now get the federal plumbing and farmer-facing details right. If the suggestions above are incorporated, India will finally plant what Punjab has long demanded: a pro-farmer, pro-federal seed law that deters the bad actors and rewards the good.

Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman’s announcement of a tax holiday from FY 2026-27 to FY 2067-2047 for foreign companies providing cloud services using Indian data centres has been interpreted as a reassurance to hyperscalers worried about permanent establishment risk. On the surface, that reading is correct. However, a deeper look reveals that the development masks a more interesting economic dynamic. 

Here's #ThePrintOpinion by KBS Sidhu @kbssidhu1961 

Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman’s announcement of a tax holiday from FY 2026-27 to FY 2067-2047 for foreign companies providing cloud services using Indian data centres has been interpreted as a reassurance to hyperscalers worried about permanent establishment risk. On the surface, that reading is correct.

However, a deeper look reveals that the development masks a more interesting economic dynamic. This measure will reshape the sharing of additional profits across the entire cloud value chain in India, benefiting not just the foreign tech giants, but also domestic data centre operators, Indian resellers, and—in ways often overlooked—Indian and global customers of cloud services.

The Budget 2026 exemption, on the face of it, applies to any foreign company earning “by procuring data centre services from a specified data centre” in India, with an exemption valid till March 2047. On first read, it seems to be a comfort measure for multinational companies such as AWS (Amazon), Microsoft, Google and Meta. Following several Supreme Court of India rulings, these companies feared that locating substantial infrastructure in India would trigger permanent establishment status, thus exposing them to Indian taxation on their global cloud revenues.

But here is the underlying operative constraint—the data centre must be owned and operated by an Indian company, notified under an approved scheme by the IT ministry. And, any sales to Indian customers must flow through an Indian reseller entity, typically the Indian subsidiary of the cloud firm or a domestic partner, which remains fully taxable in India with a 15 per cent safe harbour margin on costs.

What the Budget has done, in other words, is to trade away a potential tax claim on foreign cloud income in exchange for irreversible hard investment on Indian soil. The foreign company pays zero tax on a particular income stream; India ensures that data centre ownership, reseller involvement and domestic value-addition remain tethered to domestic companies, with massive, high-cost infrastructure on Indian soil.

Who benefits, and why the sequencing matters 

The primary beneficiary, as intended, is the foreign hyperscaler. AWS, Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud and Meta have collectively announced around $67.5 billion of data centre and AI-related investments in India over the next five years. The tax holiday reduces their after-tax cost of using Indian capacity relative to hosting the same workloads in Singapore, the UAE or Europe, making India far more competitive for global cloud workloads. 

But the chain reaction begins here. The foreign cloud’s improved after-tax return immediately raises its willingness-to-pay for Indian data centre capacity. In a market where power, cooling and suitable land are scarce—as India races to build gigawatt-scale compute infrastructure—that willingness-to-pay gets reflected in higher lease rates and better contract terms negotiated with Indian data centre operators.

Those operators are India’s emerging infrastructure barons—AdaniConneX (targeting 1 GW capacity), Reliance Jio, Tata group platforms, Airtel’s Nxtra (commanding 15 per cent market share), Yotta Infrastructure, CtrlS, Sify and others. They are racing to create AI-ready facilities across Mumbai, Chennai, Hyderabad, Visakhapatnam, Noida and Pune. The tax holiday does not directly benefit them—they continue to pay corporate tax as usual—but it indirectly bolsters their negotiating position and pricing power by making foreign customers more willing to pay premium rates for access to “specified” notified facilities.

In global data centre markets, lease rates have risen sharply over 2023–2025 because AI and cloud demand have outstripped available power and cooling and, of course, high-performance GPUs. India’s operators, now assured that their primary foreign customers enjoy long-duration tax certainty, can capture a meaningful share of the additional profits generated by this bold income tax holiday through higher capacity pricing, coming on top of India’s ambitious Superconductor Mission, which envisages up to 50 per cent open-ended capital subsidy for domestic manufacturing of GPUs.

The reseller ecosystem and cloud customers 

The Budget structure mandates that Indian reseller entities—AWS India, Microsoft India, Google Cloud India, cloud arms of IT majors like TCS, Infosys and Wipro, and telecom-embedded providers—be part of the sales chain when claiming the exemption for Indian customer sales. The 15 per cent safe harbour rules, also a part of this Budget, on related-party data centre service costs signal policy comfort with a layered value chain and protect reseller margins.

Indian and global consumers of cloud services—startups, SMEs, enterprises and SaaS firms—stand to benefit from the competitive intensity that this tax holiday catalyses. As competition among hyperscalers deepens and capacity expands, some of the additional profits will pass through as more competitive cloud pricing, lowering barriers to digital adoption and improving margins for businesses reliant on India-hosted infrastructure. 

The political economy of how this is presented matters. Announcing a “tax holiday for foreign cloud providers till 2047 reads as a necessary course correction; announcing what the opposition could frame as “20-year tax holiday for data centre conglomerates like Adani, Reliance and Tata” would draw harsher scrutiny. By routing the direct benefit through the foreign entity while hard-wiring Indian ownership, the government has elegantly packaged a very substantial infrastructure incentive inside a narrative of global openness.

This is a political skill. But it is worth being explicit: the Budget’s measure is as much about anchoring hard assets and Indian ownership as it is about welcoming foreign clouds.

Why long-term certainty was necessary

There is, however, a compelling policy case—and indeed, this bold and substantial income tax holiday is quite justified. Data centres are the physical backbone of cloud computing and AI. As workloads grow heavier, hosting capacity within national borders becomes a question of digital sovereignty. India has already moved in that direction through data localisation norms and the Digital Personal Data Protection Act.

The Budget’s tax holiday is a fiscal complement to that regulatory thrust: it says to foreign clouds, “Bring compute and workloads to India; we will not use the tax system to ambush you”—but Indian ownership and domestic intermediaries remain non-negotiable.

Viewed this way, the measure is not a disguised giveaway but a conscious, well-crafted and necessary concession: India forgoes contested tax claims in exchange for encouraging irreversible hard investment, in the order of billions of dollars, on Indian soil. That is reasonable for a country betting on becoming a global cloud hub and a centre of AI capability. 

The winners are multiple: foreign hyperscalers gain tax certainty; Indian data centre operators gain pricing power and volume; Indian resellers gain regulated margins and market growth; cloud customers gain access to cheaper, more competitive services anchored in India. It is a policy that aligns incentives across the entire value chain while preserving domestic ownership and taxable profit pools.

The packaging is clever. The economics are sound.

The framework brings together the IT Act, 2000, Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), 2023, IT Rules, 2021, the 2026 IT Rules amendments, and the IndiaAI Governance Guidelines to strengthen digital safety and platform accountability.

Key highlights:

🔹 Mandatory AI Labelling: Platforms must clearly label AI-generated or synthetic content with traceable metadata so users can identify manipulated content and prevent deception.

🔹 Fastest Takedown Timelines Yet: Removal of unlawful content after a valid government or court notice has been reduced from 36 hours to just 3 hours. Grievance redressal timelines have also been tightened—from 72 hours to 36 hours, and 24 hours to 2 hours for sensitive content such as nudity, impersonation and similar categories.

🔹 IT Act, 2000: Covers penalties for computer-related offences, identity theft (Sec. 66C), online impersonation (66D), privacy violations (66E), publishing obscene or sexually explicit content (Secs. 67 & 67A), empowers blocking of unlawful content under Sec. 69A, removal directions under Sec. 79, and enables police investigation under Secs. 78 & 80.

🔹 Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023: Covers cheating by personation (Sec. 319), forgery through false electronic records (Sec. 336), spreading false reports or misinformation causing public mischief (Sec. 353), and organised cybercrime involving deepfake content (Sec. 111).

🔹 Strict Platform Obligations: Intermediaries must not host or share content that infringes rights, invades privacy, promotes hate or violence, harms children, violates intellectual property, misleads users about message origin, knowingly spreads false information, impersonates individuals (including using AI), threatens India's sovereignty, security or public order, or violates any applicable law.

🔹 Greater Accountability for Social Media Platforms: Significant Social Media Intermediaries (SSMIs) must assist law enforcement in tracing originators of serious content, deploy automated tools to detect unlawful content, publish compliance reports, appoint grievance and compliance officers, maintain India-based compliance infrastructure, and provide user verification, appeals and fair hearing mechanisms.

🔹 Zero Tolerance for Harmful AI: Platforms are now explicitly required to prevent AI-generated child sexual abuse material, non-consensual intimate imagery, deepfakes, AI impersonation, harmful synthetic media and other unlawful AI-generated content using reasonable technical measures and automated detection systems.

🔹 Legal Consequences: Failure to comply with the IT Rules can result in intermediaries losing their Section 79 safe-harbour protection, exposing them to prosecution and legal action under applicable laws.

🔹 Robust Enforcement Ecosystem: The framework will be enforced through Grievance Appellate Committees (GACs), the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), the SAHYOG Portal, the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal, and law enforcement agencies. Citizens can report cybercrime and deepfakes through the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal, with Helpline 1930 available for cyber fraud complaints.

🔹 Responsible AI Development: Under the IndiaAI Mission, the government is funding indigenous AI safety projects, including Saakshya (IIT Jodhpur & IIT Madras), AI Vishleshak, and IIT Kharagpur's Real-Time Voice Deepfake Detection System, alongside the India AI Governance Guidelines to promote safe, trusted and responsible AI deployment.

The message is clear: AI innovation is welcome, but deepfakes, impersonation, misinformation, child exploitation, and unlawful synthetic content will face significantly stricter regulation, faster takedowns, and stronger legal consequences than ever before.

INDIA CRACKS DOWN ON AI & DEEP FAKE. BIG TECH PUT ON NOTCE

1. What has actually changed?

The Modi government amended the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021 on 10 February 2026 specifically to deal with synthetically generated information and deepfakes.
The framework covers deceptive AI-generated audio, visual and audio-visual material.
The idea is no longer simply: remove illegal content after somebody complains.

Platforms are now being pushed towards:
identification
labelling
metadata
verification
automated detection
rapid takedown
and greater accountability for allowing unlawful AI content to spread.

2. AI CONTENT HAS TO BE IDENTIFIABLE
This is probably the biggest structural change.
AI-generated/synthetically altered material covered by the rules has to be clearly identifiable as synthetic.
Platforms/services enabling generation or alteration of such content must ensure appropriate labels or traceable identifiers/metadata.
The objective is simple:
REAL CONTENT ≠ AI CONTENT
The viewer should not have to conduct a forensic investigation to figure out whether something was artificially generated.
Important nuance

Don't say “every piece of text written using AI anywhere on the internet must carry a label.”

MeitY's FAQ clarifies that the operative 2026 SGI definition primarily targets audio, visual and audio-visual information, not ordinary AI-generated written text.
A more accurate line for your video is:
“India has mandated identification and labelling requirements for covered AI-generated synthetic media, particularly deepfake audio, images and video.”

3. THE BIG NUMBER: 36 HOURS → 3 HOURS

Previously, once an intermediary received legally valid knowledge of unlawful material through the prescribed government/court process, the compliance window could be 36 hours.

That has now been cut to:

3 HOURS

That is a 91.7% reduction in response time.

So something capable of going viral nationally during an election, riot, communal incident, stock-market panic or national-security crisis can no longer theoretically remain online for a day and a half after a valid takedown direction.

The platform has only hours.

4. AND SOME COMPLAINT WINDOWS ARE EVEN SHORTER

The government says timelines for grievance redressal have also been compressed.

According to the PIB explanation:
certain complaints earlier subject to 72 hours can now require action within 36 hours

particularly sensitive categories that earlier had a 24-hour timeline can now require action within 2 hours

This specifically matters for areas such as:

impersonation

intimate imagery

nudity

deepfake abuse

other highly sensitive material.

5. BIG TECH CAN'T JUST WAIT FOR A COMPLAINT

This is another major change.

The government says intermediaries must deploy reasonable and appropriate technical measures, including automated tools or other mechanisms, against unlawful synthetically generated content.
That means platforms are increasingly being pushed from:
REACTIVE MODERATION
to
PROACTIVE DETECTION
For Significant Social Media Intermediaries, the framework explicitly envisages technical measures to identify prohibited content, including certain forms of:

rape-related material

child sexual abuse material

repeat prohibited content

unlawful synthetic content.

6. USERS MAY HAVE TO DECLARE AI CONTENT

The synthetic-media framework also places responsibility upstream.

Major platforms can be required to ask users uploading covered content whether it is synthetically generated and then use technical systems to check that declaration.

So theoretically:
User uploads video →
declares AI/not AI →
platform checks →
synthetic material gets labelled.

The earlier draft framework explicitly envisaged this declaration + technical-verification model.

7. WHY THE METADATA PART MATTERS

A visible watermark can be:

cropped,
blurred,
edited,
screen-recorded,

reposted.

Metadata/identifiers create another layer of traceability.

The government's objective is therefore not merely:

“PUT AI GENERATED IN THE CAPTION.”
It is building a system where synthetic content can carry technological indicators allowing platforms to recognise what it is.
That becomes especially useful once the same manipulated video is downloaded and re-uploaded across multiple platforms.
8. THE RULES TARGET DEEPFAKE IMPERSONATION DIRECTLY
Existing IT Rules already prohibit users from publishing material that:

impersonates another person

misleads users about the origin of a message

knowingly spreads patently false or misleading information

threatens public order

violates another applicable law.

AI does not create an exemption.

If AI is being used for impersonation, fraud, defamatory fabrication or other unlawful activity, existing criminal and cyber provisions can also apply.

9. BNS CAN ALSO COME INTO PLAY
The PIB release specifically points towards provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita.
Depending upon what the deepfake is being used for, authorities could examine provisions relating to:
Section 319 — cheating by personation
Section 336 — forgery

Section 353 — false information/rumours capable of causing public mischief or fear

Section 111 — organised crime, where the factual circumstances justify it.

So there isn't necessarily a standalone offence called simply:

“making a deepfake.”

The legal consequence depends heavily upon what the deepfake does.

10. CHILD SEXUAL ABUSE DEEPFAKES GET SPECIAL ATTENTION
This is perhaps the least discussed but most important provision.
The amended framework explicitly covers harmful AI-generated material involving:
child sexual exploitation

non-consensual intimate imagery

impersonation

other prohibited synthetic material.

Platforms are expected to prevent such content and act rapidly when detected.

11. SOCIAL-MEDIA GIANTS HAVE EXTRA DUTIES

Platforms classified as Significant Social Media Intermediaries, broadly those crossing the prescribed Indian user threshold, face additional compliance obligations.

These include mechanisms involving:
automated detection
grievance officers
compliance officers

local points of contact

India-based compliance structures

periodic compliance reports

appeals processes

originator tracing in specified circumstances for messaging services.
So the rules are aimed not only at the person creating the deepfake.
They put a major compliance burden on the distribution network itself.
12. THE REAL STICK: SAFE HARBOUR
This is where it becomes serious for Meta, X, Google, Telegram and other intermediaries.
Section 79 of the IT Act provides intermediaries conditional protection from liability for third-party content.
But that protection depends upon complying with the law and prescribed due diligence.
The PIB release reiterates that failure to observe obligations under the IT Rules can result in the intermediary losing its Section 79 exemption, after which liability can arise under applicable law.

That makes the real equation:

Comply with due diligence → retain intermediary protection

Ignore statutory obligations → safe-harbour protection can be jeopardised

That is far more powerful than merely issuing a fine.

13. GOVERNMENT HAS BUILT A TAKEDOWN PIPELINE

There is now an increasingly integrated enforcement architecture:

Grievance Appellate Committees — GACs

Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre — I4C

SAHYOG Portal

National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal

police/cybercrime units

authorised State and Central Government agencies.

The SAHYOG system in particular enables centralised electronic communication of lawful content-removal notices to intermediaries.

14. INDIA IS ALSO BUILDING ITS OWN DEEPFAKE-DETECTION TECHNOLOGY

Under the IndiaAI Mission's Safe & Trusted AI pillar, government-backed work includes indigenous detection and governance technologies.
PIB identifies projects including:
Saakshya — multi-agent deepfake-detection framework developed by IIT Jodhpur and IIT Madras
AI Vishleshak — audio-visual forgery detection
IIT Kharagpur work on real-time voice deepfake detection.

So this is not purely a legal crackdown.

It is simultaneously a:

LEGAL + PLATFORM + TECHNOLOGICAL framework.

15. WHY THIS IS HAPPENING NOW

Generative AI has destroyed the old assumption that:
“Seeing is believing.”
Today one person can manufacture:

a politician announcing something he never said

a CEO apparently moving a stock

an Army officer issuing a fake warning

communal speeches

celebrity pornography

fake financial endorsements

fabricated battlefield footage

false evidence of violence
within minutes.
And the fake can reach millions before conventional fact-checking catches up.
Therefore the Indian approach is increasingly:
IDENTIFY → LABEL → DETECT → TRACE → REMOVE → PROSECUTE
rather than merely:
WAIT → RECEIVE COMPLAINT → INVESTIGATE.
THE BIG STORY FOR YOUR VIDEO

The headline isn't simply:

“Deepfakes must carry labels.”

The bigger story is that India is trying to change where responsibility lies.

Earlier, platforms could largely argue:

A user uploaded it; we are merely the intermediary.

The regulatory direction is increasingly:

If you operate the technology that generates, distributes or algorithmically amplifies synthetic content in India, you have duties to identify it, label it and respond rapidly when it becomes unlawful.

BREAKING FACT CHECK: Adam Schiff’s latest election alarm is built around one true fact—and several enormous omissions.

Yes, a federal judge found that USPS violated an injunction when it completed its final mail-ballot rule. Court orders must be followed while they are appealed.

But Schiff leaves out the rest:

• The ruling concerned USPS defendants—not a finding that President Trump personally violated the order.

• The mandatory system is currently blocked. A hearing on a longer injunction is scheduled for September 3.

• No evidence has been presented that millions of voters have actually been disenfranchised. That is a prediction based on an anonymous whistleblower’s concerns about testing.

• The controversy involves OUTBOUND ballots being mailed by election officials—not completed ballots cast by voters.

• Even the whistleblower’s disclosure says a rejected batch would be returned to election officials to correct and resubmit. The ballots would not simply be “discarded.”

• The published rule expressly says USPS will not verify names, addresses, citizenship or voter eligibility. It will not compare the portal data with state voter rolls.

What does the rule require? Official election-mail markings, automation-compatible envelopes, unique barcodes and auditable tracking.

If the system is rushed, test it.

If it is defective, fix it.

If the courts believe USPS lacks sufficient authority, Congress should immediately establish a lawful national standard—with proper testing and a rapid cure process that protects every eligible voter.

But do not turn an implementation problem into an excuse to kill ballot accountability.

TEST IT. FIX IT. TRACK EVERY BALLOT.

Accountability is not disenfranchisement.

text:
The smallest corporate penalty under DPDP is ₹50 crore. That is the residual entry in the Schedule, covering breach of any provision of the Act or the Rules that is not separately listed.

Set that against what compliance costs. For a mid-sized Indian company a DPDP programme runs to a few crore and takes three to four quarters end to end. Most of that time is discovery rather than remediation, because you cannot fix data flows you have not mapped and very few companies hold a current map.

The arithmetic is not close, and the pressure sits in the calendar rather than the cost.

Full enforcement begins 13 May 2027. If a programme takes three to four quarters and you want it finished rather than in progress on that date, the comfortable start date has already passed.

That does not mean a company starting now cannot get there. It means the sequence matters more than it did. Data inventory first, then a gap assessment, then remediation ordered by penalty exposure rather than by what is easiest to fix.

#DPDP #compliance #surispeaks

BIG NEWS 🚨 Login credentials of 149 mn accounts including Gmail, Facebook, Netflix leaked.

Cybersecurity researcher Jeremiah Fowler has discovered an unsecured online database.

149M credentials dumped in an unsecured 96GB database, a "dream wish list for criminals" per researcher Jeremiah Fowler, who stumbled on it while scanning open IPs. We're talking Gmail (millions affected), Facebook, Netflix, Instagram, Roblox, dating sites, even banking logins—likely scraped via infostealer malware like RedLine or Vidar infecting PCs worldwide. No owner ID'd, but it sat exposed for weeks before takedown, amplifying risks of phishing, ID theft, and account takeovers.

Strategic edge: For hackers, this is nitro fuel—credential stuffing attacks could spike 2-3x post-leak, per past patterns (e.g., 2023 RockYou2021 dump). Big Tech's response? Google/FB urging password resets + MFA, but with reuse rates still at 65% globally, it's a ticking bomb. Broader play: Echoes the 2025 mega-breach (184M passwords), showing infostealers evolving faster than defenses—malware now bypasses AV via AI obfuscation.

Indian lens: With 900M+ internet users and digital economy booming (UPI at 15B txn/month), this hits home—est. 10-15M Indian accounts exposed, fueling Aadhaar-linked fraud spikes. Post-DPDP Act rollout in '24, fines could hammer firms, but enforcement gaps persist (CERT-In handled 1.5M incidents in '25 alone). Credit Modi's cybersecurity push—NCCC upgrades cut response times 40%—but without it, we'd be replaying 2022 AIIMS hack. Atmanirbhar angle: Time to pivot to local password managers like PassBolt forks?

Without swift action, expect fraud waves. Thoughts—changed your passwords yet, or waiting for the phish?

is the ECI compromised?  
 In March 2026, ahead of the Kerala Assembly elections (polling on 9 April 2026), a 2019 Election Commission of India (ECI) letter redistributed by the Kerala Chief Electoral Officer’s (CEO) office was found to carry the seal of the BJP’s Kerala unit. This sparked a political row, followed by police-directed efforts to remove related social media posts

This takedown action itself became controversial, with critics framing it as an attempt to suppress discussion of an official lapse during an election period, while authorities maintained it was necessary to stop the circulation of a withdrawn and erroneous document that was being used to question the ECI’s credibility.The episode remained a flashpoint in the final stretch of the Kerala campaign, with the ECI treating it as a corrected administrative mistake and the opposition presenting it as evidence of deeper concerns about the poll body’s independence.The letter and the seal
The document was an ECI communication dated 19 March 2019 containing guidelines/FAQs on the publicity of candidates’ criminal antecedents (following a Supreme Court judgment). CPI(M) and Congress shared versions online showing the BJP Kerala unit’s seal. It had been circulated by the Kerala CEO’s office to political parties, District Election Officers, and Returning Officers as part of clarifications around mid-March 2026.thesouthfirst.comKerala CEO / ECI explanation:
It was described as a “purely clerical error.” The BJP Kerala unit had approached the CEO’s office seeking clarification on the (by then revised) 2019 guidelines and submitted a photocopy of the original directive that already bore the party’s seal. Staff overlooked this and redistributed that version. The error was identified; on 21 March a formal withdrawal notice was issued telling recipients to disregard the document. An Assistant Section Officer was suspended pending inquiry. Later, a Deputy CEO and a Section Officer were relieved of election-related duties.livemint.comOpposition parties (CPI(M) and Congress) rejected the clerical-error account. They alleged compromised institutional neutrality, claiming seals were being “casually swapped” and questioning whether the ECI and BJP shared the same “power centre.” Some BJP responses labelled the circulation of the old document as misinformation or a political plot.thewire.inDeletion of posts controversyActing on an ECI directive (under the Model Code of Conduct), the Kerala Police cyber cell issued notices to X (Twitter), Facebook, Instagram, and numerous individual accounts. They demanded removal of posts sharing the letter that carried the BJP seal.  Police argued the content insulted the Election Commission, undermined its integrity and transparency, spread false claims about a rectified clerical error, and risked public order or communal harmony by potentially fuelling political division. text:
*Elon Musk’s Starlink was trying to beat Jio in India*

*But Jio used its 1st mover’s advantage to stop them in their tracks*

*The SHOCKER? Indian Gov is changing a 138 year old law that will bring Starlink back in the game*

*Here’s how Elon is rethinking internet & can possibly kill Jio:*

In 2016, when most of us were witnessing a business disruption standing in queues to get our hands on the free Jio sim card,

12,869 miles away at Rocket Road, California, a group of engineers were planning a technological disruption.

Their goal? Rethink internet access.

Their solution? Satellite Internet.

Traditionally, we have been using internet that relies on cable wires, fiber optic lines, or cellular networks.

But making cable wires or fiber optic lines available in remote villages and hard terrains is not only costly but highly impractical as well.

And this is where satellite internet and Starlink by Elon Musk comes in.

Satellite Internet uses signals from satellites orbiting the Earth.

And Starlink is a collection of thousands of small satellites orbiting around 350 miles above the Earth.

For the satellite internet to work, the user on the ground connects to the Starlink dish, known as the user terminal.

The user terminal communicates with nearby Starlink satellites and forms a link to the larger Starlink network

The satellites then form a mesh network, that allows them to pass data between each other and create global network coverage.

Starlink’s motto is — ‘virtually anywhere on earth without wires or cellphone towers.’

It started its operation in 2019 and true to its motto, it’s already available in over 65 countries,

— covering all 7 continents (including Antarctica!)

But Starlink hasn’t been able to make any progress in India.

Last year, it registered its business in India via a local unit Starlink Satellite Communications Pvt Ltd.

The company had planned to provide fast internet data in the Indian market at a subsidized price compared to the international market.

It had received 5,000+ pre-orders.

But the government said Starlink Internet Services doesn’t have the license to offer services in India.

And it asked Starlink to return people’s money.

Now, one company’s loss is another company’s gain.

In Feb this year, Reliance Jio partnered up with Luxembourg-based SES to provide satellite-based broadband services in India.

And created a joint venture called — Jio Space Technology Ltd.

Moreover, Starlink and Jio Space aren’t the only contenders for India’s space spectrum.

OneWeb is backed by Airtel in India and Hughes Communication.

Tata group entity Nelco partnered up with Canada's Telesat.

And Amazon’s Kuiper is going to launch satellites in 2024.

But why are so many companies vying for India’s space spectrum?

India has a population of 1.4 billion out of which 40% do not have internet access because they are in rural and remote areas.

And traditional terrestrial networks are not easy to install.

Hence, India’s satellite broadband service is expected to reach $1.9 billion by 2030, growing at a CAGR of 36%.

Now, because India has so many contenders for its spectrum, the question arises — who should get it?

Starlink and OneWeb wanted the government to assign licenses to companies, since spectrum is a natural resource that should be shared by companies.

But Jio wanted the government to auction the spectrum like it did with 4G & 5G 👀

Finally, the government brought in some reforms and firstly dedicated a sole agency IN-SPACe to authorize space activities for both government and private satellite communication companies.

And a bill has been proposed to replace the 138-year-old Indian Telegraph Act that currently governs the telecommunication sector.

So now, both Jio Space & OneWeb have received their GMPCS license from the Department of Telecommunications in India.

And Starlink is 3rd in line to receive the GMPCS license.

IFF believes the findings must be placed before the Court, the 2,873-person list must be independently audited, and facial recognition at peaceful assemblies must be suspended until India has a rights-respecting statutory framework governing biometric surveillance.
